brief.head: Friends of choice
brief.text: Amit Varma was a loner until early adult­hood. The in­ter­net gave him com­mu­ni­ties of choice[[x2]][[x3]]: he and Ajay Shah, both in Bombay, met on­line, though not on a dat­ing app. {118-S08}

brief.head: The easy exit
brief.text: One stu­dent told a sur­vey, Amit Varma re­called, that she used apps rather than date a class­mate she might later see every day “with an­other girl”. {118-S09}

brief.head: Same age in public
brief.text: Studies say women seek men their own age. A friend told Amit Varma that was for ap­pear­ances; pri­vately, she prefers men much older or much younger. {118-S10}

brief.head: Lost in the manosphere
brief.text: Twenty-five years ago Amit Varma read Neil Strauss’s *The Game*, a pickup artists’ hand­book. Its world is now an in­dus­try, and many of its men have given up on love. {118-S11}

brief.head: The great mystery
brief.text: Georges Simenon, one of Amit Varma’s favourite nov­el­ists, said the theme run­ning through all his work was that no per­son can fully com­mu­ni­cate him­self to an­other[[x10]]. {118-J22}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on men, women and data
lead.head: Dance like no one’s searching

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 118

body: Ask peo­ple what they want and you get their stated pref­er­ences. Watch what they type into a search box, or whom they swipe right on, and you see some­thing closer to the truth.
That was the bet as Amit Varma and Ajay Shah turned their pas­sion for mea­sure­ment on men and women.

The sub­ject was split off from their pre­vi­ous episode on data, which, Shah said, “would have been five hours” on its own. Inside the team, he added, Varma is known as the Energiser Bunny, “be­cause he goes on and on”.
## Who is choos­ing?
Varma began with an old col­umn of his, which ar­gued that India’s ris­ing di­vorce rates were “a damn good thing”: more women had the agency to leave bad mar­riages.
A friend, Hamsini Hariharan, had sug­gested a stranger met­ric still. More women in prison, Varma said, means more women with agency and the op­por­tu­nity to go out in the world. {118-C01}
The test, the hosts agreed, is who re­ally de­cides. A man who down­loads a gro­cery app may sim­ply hand the phone to his wife and pay for what­ever she picks.
## The se­cret self

The heart of the episode was Seth Stephens-Davidowitz’s *Everybody Lies*, which Varma called a phe­nom­e­nal book. Its premise is that peo­ple are most truly them­selves when search­ing on­line, be­cause they are anony­mous and no­body is watch­ing.
Varma in­voked Gabriel García Márquez’s three selves: a pub­lic self, a pri­vate self known to a few in­ti­mates, and a se­cret self known “to no­body ex­cept Google Baba”. {118-C03}

That se­cret self, the data sug­gests, frets most about sex. Searches for “sex­less mar­riage” far out­num­ber those for “un­happy mar­riage”, and par­ents are like­lier than the child­less to con­fess re­gret to Google.
Shah drew a broader les­son. The hosts live in a bub­ble, he said, whereas “this data re­flects the me­dian Indian”, who is “a very dif­fer­ent per­son from us”.
## Swipe right, then what?

Dating apps, Varma ar­gued, moved ro­mance from com­mu­ni­ties of cir­cum­stance, fixed by ge­og­ra­phy, school and work, to com­mu­ni­ties of choice. “If you are a gay per­son say born in 1960, you could spend your whole life alone,” he said. One born in 2000 is not going to. {118-C08}

Choice has also brought in­equal­ity. Women swipe right on far fewer pro­files than men, so a few men get most of the at­ten­tion. Varma cited a Tinder Gini co­ef­fi­cient of 0.58, “more in­equal­ity than 95 per cent of the coun­tries in the world”. {118-C09}

Shah asked what had changed, since de­sire has prob­a­bly not al­tered in 65,000 years. Varma’s an­swer was that with a mil­lion pro­files to choose from, ev­ery­one be­comes super se­lec­tive. “The in­stincts were al­ways the same be­cause they are what they are, but the be­hav­iours have changed.”
Shah saw a les­son for mea­sure­ment. A satel­lite pho­tograph­ing North Korea at night changes noth­ing there. Dating apps made ro­mance ob­serv­able and “com­pletely changed the sys­tem as well”.

Finally, the hosts turned to a Facebook index of friend­ship be­tween the sexes, which *The Economist* pro­posed to name after *When Harry Met Sally*. India scored 0.35. Shah called the sep­a­ra­tion of men and women in India “a so­cial cri­sis”. {118-C15}
Varma closed on a larger mys­tery. Many econ­o­mists, he said, are work­ing on the wrong things. “We don’t un­der­stand our­selves. We don’t un­der­stand other peo­ple.”

second.label: Search and politics
second.head: Word order wins the vote
second.deck: Amit Varma on how Google searches read America’s voters before the polls did

pic.caption: Donald Trump in his official second-term presidential portrait, 2025

body: Donald Trump’s rise in 2016 took many peo­ple aback. But Amit Varma, retelling the work of Seth Stephens-Davidowitz, said Google had seen it com­ing four years ear­lier: many searched for a racial slur along­side Obama’s vic­tory, in­stead of “first black pres­i­dent”, in the states that later voted a par­tic­u­lar way. {#trump}

After the most re­cent US elec­tion, Stephens-Davidowitz wrote in *The Economist* that a look at Google beat all the sur­veys on the tele­vi­sion news. In states where peo­ple searched for the “Trump Harris de­bate”, Trump won. Where they searched for the “Harris Trump de­bate”, Harris won. {118-S05}
No per­son would think to look for such a sig­nal, Varma said, but ma­chines un­leashed on the data find it.

quote.text: Just that word order. And it’s such a sub­tle thing.

third.head: Cold comfort for women

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the office thermostat

body: Amit Varma has a new mea­sure of women’s em­pow­er­ment, drawn from a very old ob­ser­va­tion: the de­fault tem­per­a­ture of of­fice air con­di­tion­ing.

When air con­di­tion­ing be­came com­mon in of­fices in the 1950s and 60s, he said, it was de­signed for men in suits. Men have a dif­fer­ent meta­bolic rate and pre­fer it colder, so a tem­per­a­ture nor­mal for him would be too cold for a woman. {118-S03}
Hence an ar­gu­ment he sus­pects every mar­ried cou­ple has had: the wife says she is cold, and the hus­band tells her to put on a sweater. {#sweater}
Varma would like the de­fault to rise a lit­tle, until men and women are both com­fort­able. He ad­mit­ted he does not know how to mea­sure it at scale, and asked view­ers for met­rics of their own.

p2.title: The hidden heart
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what empowerment metrics, search data, dating apps and Facebook reveal about men and women

quote.text: More women in pris­ons is a good thing be­cause it means more women have agency

box.title: A book of secret searches
box.text: *Everybody Lies*, by Seth Stephens-Davidowitz, uses anonymised searches to study human na­ture[[x5]]. Amit Varma called it phe­nom­e­nal, and read many of its find­ings from his essay *The Truth About Ourselves*. Its premise: the se­cret self shows when we search. {118-C03}

sections.label: Empowerment
sections.head: More divorces, please
sections.caption: metrics of empowerment
body: Amit Varma’s start­ing point was a col­umn he wrote many years ago ar­gu­ing that India’s ris­ing di­vorce rates were a good thing[[x1]]. “Rising di­vorce rates are a sign of women’s em­pow­er­ment,” he said. {118-S01}

The idea grew into an episode of his pod­cast *The Seen and the Unseen*, “Metrics of Empowerment”, in which he and three friends hunted for un­usual num­bers. Solo travel by women was one, and Varma re­ports it is ris­ing. Nidhi Gupta sug­gested count­ing the fam­i­lies whose last child is a boy. Hamsini Hariharan sug­gested count­ing women in prison.
## The hand on the phone
Some num­bers that sound good can de­ceive. In tra­di­tional fam­i­lies, a man who down­loads the BigBasket app may sim­ply hand the phone to his wife to choose the gro­ceries, and pay.

Ajay Shah of­fered an ex­am­ple from the hosts’ Life Lessons course. Someone de­cides to have pizza, some­one de­cides on Domino’s, and some­one places the order. If the men make the first two de­ci­sions, the woman tap­ping the app shows noth­ing about her agency. {118-S02}

Even ris­ing in­comes can mis­lead. Women’s par­tic­i­pa­tion in India’s labour force rose and then dipped dras­ti­cally, Varma said, stress­ing that the causes are many. One is that some fam­i­lies, once they reached a cer­tain in­come, felt that a work­ing wife “af­fects the fam­ily hon­our”. {118-C02}
~ Varma asked view­ers for em­pow­er­ment met­rics of their own. Two-wheeler and car own­er­ship by women, he noted, are among the stan­dard ones.

sections.label: The secret self
sections.head: Google Baba knows best
sections.caption: what our searches reveal
body: *Everybody Lies*, Amit Varma said, rests on one idea: peo­ple are most truly them­selves when they search on­line[[x6]], be­cause no­body is watch­ing. It is where, in Gabriel García Márquez’s scheme, the se­cret self shows.

Its au­thor, Seth Stephens-Davidowitz, drew on anonymised data from Google, Facebook and Pornhub. Facebook it­self shows the op­po­site face: it is, in his words, “dig­i­tal brag-to-my-friends-about-how-good-my-life-is serum”. {118-J17}
## What the search box hears
The top com­plaint about mar­riage, the searches sug­gest, is a lack of sex. There are 16 times more com­plaints about a spouse not want­ing sex than about one not will­ing to talk. {118-C04}
Varma stressed that what peo­ple search for or fan­ta­sise about has noth­ing to do with what they would want in the real world.

Parents are two and a half times more likely to ask whether a son is gifted than a daugh­ter, though young girls have larger vo­cab­u­lar­ies and are more often in gifted pro­grammes. Varma imag­ines the bias is far worse in India. {118-C05}
~ Many of us, he said, never re­veal our true selves to any­one, not even to our­selves. And some­one who hides that self can never be truly loved. {118-C06}

quote.text: Searches for sex­less mar­riage are three and a half times more com­mon than un­happy mar­riage, and eight times more com­mon than love­less mar­riage.

art.caption: Amit Varma on what our searches reveal

sections.label: The swipe economy
sections.head: A million to choose from
sections.caption: what dating apps tell us
body: Ajay Shah asked the awk­ward ques­tion. Male and fe­male de­sire, he said, “have prob­a­bly not changed in 65,000 years”. So what is new? {#years}

Amit Varma, de­scrib­ing rather than en­dors­ing, said a bi­ol­o­gist would tell you men are wired to seek youth and beauty, and women sta­tus and af­flu­ence. In a small cir­cle, or­di­nary men found part­ners. On an app, “I have a mil­lion peo­ple to choose from.” {118-C10}

Marriage, he ar­gued, was an un­easy equi­lib­rium from a time when peo­ple met few oth­ers: a bun­dle of love, sex, com­pan­ion­ship, friend­ship[[x7]] and shared par­ent­hood. Nobody has worked out how to live once it is un­bun­dled[[x8]].
## A cold equi­lib­rium

Varma read a tweet by Rob Henderson, who coined the term lux­ury be­liefs. Men high on the dark triad of psy­chopa­thy, nar­cis­sism and Machiavellianism, per­haps 10 to 20 per cent of users, mis­treat women, who then mis­treat or­di­nary men, who in turn mis­treat or­di­nary women. {118-C11}
~ Many are drop­ping out. In one sur­vey, Varma said, three in ten men and one in four women had not had sex in a year: a sex re­ces­sion, as the term now goes. {118-C13}

quote.text: Bad be­hav­iour drives out the good.
quote.who: Rob Henderson, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The friendship index
sections.head: Friends by the billion
sections.caption: the When Harry Met Sally index
body: Amit Varma loves *When Harry Met Sally*, a charm­ing film, he said, and he had a crush on Meg Ryan. {118-R24}
Its premise, as Billy Crystal’s char­ac­ter tells Meg Ryan’s, is that men and women can’t be friends, be­cause “the sex part al­ways gets in the way”.

Facebook has now put a num­ber on it. A study of 1.8 bil­lion adult users and 1.4 tril­lion links be­tween them pro­duced a cross-gender friend­ship index, which *The Economist* pro­posed to call the When Harry Met Sally Index.
Varma had been call­ing it the Whimsy Index, until he re­alised the I al­ready stands for index: the When Harry Met Sally Index Index. {118-J12}
## Higher than ex­pected

Zero means the sexes are en­tirely seg­re­gated; one means as many friends of the other sex as of one’s own. India scored 0.35, which sur­prised Varma, given how awk­ward Indian men are with women. {#india}
Ajay Shah was ex­cited that the data goes down to the small­est ad­min­is­tra­tive units, so re­searchers could study the sep­a­ra­tion of the sexes city by city and dis­trict by dis­trict.

~ Shah also read a pas­sage from Ford Madox Ford’s *Parade’s End*: lovers must wait to­gether “for a week, for a year, for a life­time” be­fore the final in­ti­mate con­ver­sa­tion. “Beautiful,” Varma replied. “You have a ro­man­tic soul in you.” {118-R27}

quote.text: The pur­dah that we have in India that the two gen­ders stand apart is some­thing that is just com­pletely bro­ken.

art.caption: Amit Varma (right) on the When Harry Met Sally index, with Ajay Shah

quote.text: We can never truly know an­other per­son. I would argue at one level we can never truly know our­selves. These are the great prob­lems of hu­man­ity.

p3.title: Tales from the data
p3.deck: What searches, swipes and a pavement camera say about us

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s home experiment with Google autocomplete
stories.head: What husbands want, by country
body: Amit Varma has an ex­per­i­ment you can carry out at home. Open an incog­nito win­dow, so that Google’s au­to­com­plete is not coloured by what you have searched be­fore, type the start of a sen­tence and see how the world fin­ishes it. Better still, use a VPN to pre­tend to be some­where else.

When Seth Stephens-Davidowitz wrote *Everybody Lies*, the top com­ple­tion in India of “my hus­band wants” was a wish to be breast­fed. The book re­ports that porn searches for women breast­feed­ing men are four times higher in India and Bangladesh than any­where else. {118-S06}
“I sim­ply don’t get this,” Varma said. He had tried to work out the cul­tural rea­sons, and could not.
Times change. When Varma tried it, breast­feed­ing had slipped to num­ber two. Number one was “my hus­band wants me to serve his mis­tress”.

Then he set his VPN to Australia, as he does to watch cy­cling on SBS. There, hus­bands wanted an open mar­riage, a sec­ond wife, and some­thing far stranger. One com­ple­tion was “an open mar­riage novel”. “Australians want to read books about the things that they are both­ered about,” Varma con­cluded. {118-J05}
Ajay Shah won­dered whether VPNs could com­pare the states of India. Varma’s VPN only does coun­tries, but he thought there might be a re­search project in it.
~ The point, he said, is that any­one can try this: “you don’t have to be a priv­i­leged re­cip­i­ent of anonymised data from Google.”
stories.why: Basic urges are shared, Varma sug­gested, but cul­ture shapes how they show up. A search box, read coun­try by coun­try, is a free win­dow into pri­vate pre­oc­cu­pa­tions, and any­one can open it.
stories.postscript: Also from Varma’s searches: “is my hus­band gay” is far more pop­u­lar than “is my hus­band cheat­ing”.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Google autocomplete test

stories.kicker: Malini Goyal’s Tinder data, as told by Amit Varma
stories.head: Delhi waits, Bangalore doesn’t
body: For their book *Unboxing Bengaluru*, Malini Goyal and her co-author looked at Tinder data from Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore, mea­sur­ing how long matched users took to go to each other’s homes.

In Delhi it took months, in Mumbai weeks, in Bangalore days. Amit Varma of­fered rea­sons: Delhi is a low-trust so­ci­ety, hous­ing in Mumbai is at a pre­mium, and many sin­gles in Bangalore live alone. {118-S12}
Then Goyal went out and spoke to users. Among them, Varma said, “the promis­cu­ity was off the charts, but no­body was happy”. {#happy}

~ Back in the day, you fell for some­one, had an ar­gu­ment, came back and tried to work things through. Today ten other matches are chat­ting in real time, and if some­thing is mildly wrong with one per­son, you move on.
stories.why: Building a re­la­tion­ship means work­ing through fric­tion. An app with ten al­ter­na­tives al­ways wait­ing makes leav­ing eas­ier than stay­ing, Varma sug­gested, and too much choice can leave peo­ple jaded rather than happy.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Tinder in three cities

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s unbuilt measure of women’s freedom
stories.head: Who walks home after dark?
body: Ajay Shah has a mea­sure­ment idea he has not yet built, but thinks is fea­si­ble and worth doing: fix a cam­era with a tele­photo lens out­side a win­dow, framed on the pave­ment.
Code would count the peo­ple in the frame and clas­sify their gen­der. That yields two num­bers: the share of peo­ple in pub­lic who are women, and how that share tails off as evening comes in.

Shah, who has worked on crime vic­tim­i­sa­tion sur­veys, links it to a ques­tion put to par­ents: what time should their teenage daugh­ter be back home?[[x11]] The an­swer re­flects so­cial mores and how safe par­ents think the streets are. {#daughter}
~ It is, he said, “a lit­tle piece of soft­ware that needs to be built”. Then cam­eras around the world could be “qui­etly purring”, pro­duc­ing daily data on women in the pub­lic square. {118-S04}
stories.why: How many women are out in pub­lic, es­pe­cially after dark, is a sim­ple, con­tin­u­ous mea­sure of how free a so­ci­ety is. With today’s image clas­si­fiers, Shah sug­gested, it is within easy reach.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the camera on the pavement

stories.kicker: Amit Varma, a provocative column and the search data
stories.head: Buyer’s remorse in the nursery
body: Amit Varma once wrote a col­umn ar­gu­ing that it is im­moral to have chil­dren[[x9]], partly to be provoca­tive. A lot of par­ents, he said, got re­ally angry.

Only after read­ing *Everybody Lies* did he un­der­stand why. People are seven times more likely to ask Google whether they will re­gret not hav­ing chil­dren than whether they will re­gret hav­ing them. That much, he said, is what you would ex­pect.
The sec­ond fig­ure is not. “Adults with chil­dren are three point six times more likely to tell Google they re­gret their de­ci­sion than are adults with­out chil­dren,” Varma read out. {118-S07}
~ “So full buyer’s re­morse hap­pen­ing,” he said, “if you can call par­ent­ing buy­ing.” {118-J08}
stories.why: What peo­ple say about par­ent­hood in pub­lic and what they type alone can be very dif­fer­ent. A fierce back­lash may be a sign that an ar­gu­ment has touched a pri­vate re­gret.

quiz.q: Which word order in searches tracked Trump’s wins in the most recent US election?
quiz.a: States search­ing “Trump Harris de­bate” went to Trump; “Harris Trump de­bate”, to Harris.

quiz.q: In Malini Goyal’s Tinder data, how quickly did Bangalore matches get to each other’s homes?
quiz.a: Within days, against weeks in Mumbai and months in Delhi.

quiz.q: Which unusual sign of women’s empowerment did Hamsini Hariharan suggest counting?
quiz.a: Women in pris­ons: more of them means more agency and op­por­tu­nity.

quiz.q: What does Ajay Shah call the separation of men and women in India?
quiz.a: A so­cial cri­sis, a pur­dah that in­ter­feres with the emer­gence of the good so­ci­ety.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, do offices often feel too cold for women?
quiz.a: Office air con­di­tion­ing, from the 1950s and 60s, was de­signed for men in suits.

quiz.q: What is the Tinder Gini coefficient, and how does it compare with countries?
quiz.a: 0.58, more un­equal than 95 per cent of the coun­tries in the world.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 118. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Donald Trump (Daniel Torok, public domain); Ford Madox Ford (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Georges Simenon (Studio Harcourt., public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.why: An economist’s view of the puz­zle of women’s labour-force par­tic­i­pa­tion in India.

shelf.title: Crime Victimisation in India
shelf.creator: Edited by Ajay Shah et al
shelf.why: Source of the sur­vey ques­tion about what time par­ents think their teenage daugh­ter should be home, which he treats as a mea­sure of women’s em­pow­er­ment.

shelf.title: Google Trends
shelf.creator: Google
shelf.why: You can save a search as a fixed URL and rerun it to see what the world is pay­ing at­ten­tion to over time.

shelf.title: Google Autocomplete experiments (incognito window, optionally with a VPN)
shelf.creator: Google
shelf.why: In an incog­nito win­dow au­to­com­plete isn’t bi­ased by your his­tory, and a VPN shows other countries’ re­sults.

shelf.title: Adolescence
shelf.creator: Jack Thorne & Stephen Graham
shelf.why: A TV se­ries whose one-take for­mat lets the ac­tion un­fold or­gan­i­cally, which Amit calls a new pin­na­cle in film­mak­ing and a story about the human con­di­tion, not ei­ther side’s pol­i­tics.

shelf.title: The Game
shelf.creator: Neil Strauss
shelf.why: It is a ma­nip­u­la­tive pickup-artist hand­book but shows a real un­der­stand­ing of human na­ture, and helps ex­plain where today’s manosphere came from.

shelf.title: Rob Henderson’s tweet on dark triad men and dating apps
shelf.creator: Rob Henderson
shelf.why: Amit calls it fan­tas­tic.

shelf.title: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs — Ep 46 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On be­liefs im­ported from rich-world dis­course that make their hold­ers feel vir­tu­ous while hurt­ing the peo­ple they claim to help, such as the min­i­mum wage, or op­pos­ing sweat­shops that beat every other op­tion work­ers have.

shelf.title: The Romantic Recession report
shelf.why: It doc­u­ments fall­ing trust among sin­gles: women avoid­ing dat­ing strangers, and men feel­ing women don’t give them a fair chance.

shelf.title: Studies on dating trends (Pew 2023, SoulMatcher 2025, OkCupid 2017, GDI 2025, Tinder 2025, IJCHP 2024)
shelf.why: Sources for the find­ings on age pref­er­ences, swipe rates and the Tinder Gini co­ef­fi­cient.

shelf.title: The World in 2050 — Ep 106 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A play­ful but se­ri­ous at­tempt to imag­ine the world 25 years out, from swarms of cheap drones in war to how re­la­tion­ships might be or­gan­ised once love, sex, com­pan­ion­ship and par­ent­ing come apart.

shelf.title: Malini Goyal is the Curious One — Ep 377 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Malini Goyal
shelf.why: Journalist Malini Goyal on Bangalore: her di­ag­no­sis of a city with 5G soft­ware and 2G hard­ware, and her re­search on its dat­ing cul­ture, which found that when ev­ery­one has ten choices, peo­ple who want a part­ner to grow with strug­gle to find one.

shelf.title: Unboxing Bengaluru
shelf.creator: Malini Goyal & Prashanth Prakash
shelf.why: A book on Bangalore with a line Amit loves: its soft­ware is 5G but its hard­ware 2G, a fail­ure of gov­er­nance.

shelf.title: Finding Love in Modern India — Ep 401 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Sanjana Ramachandran
shelf.why: A de­tailed look at how hard dat­ing apps are, and how they are hard in dif­fer­ent ways for men and women.

shelf.title: Famous Last Questions
shelf.creator: Sanjana Ramachandran
shelf.why: A longer treat­ment of mod­ern Indian dat­ing.

shelf.title: When Harry Met Sally
shelf.creator: Rob Reiner
shelf.why: Amit loves it and calls it a charm­ing film.

shelf.title: The Facebook study on Cross-Gender Social Ties
shelf.why: Ajay is ex­cited be­cause the data goes down to the small­est ad­min­is­tra­tive units.

shelf.title: Can men and women be just friends?
shelf.creator: The Economist
shelf.why: It ex­plains the Facebook index and pro­poses nam­ing it after When Harry Met Sally.

shelf.title: Parade’s End
shelf.creator: Ford Madox Ford
shelf.why: The pas­sage ar­gues that real in­ti­mate con­ver­sa­tion needs years of liv­ing to­gether.

shelf.title: Gurwinder Bhogal quoting Christ Williamson on hiding your true self
shelf.creator: Gurwinder Bhogal
shelf.why: It links search data, where people’s hid­den selves show up, to a point about why being au­then­tic mat­ters for being loved.

shelf.title: Novels of Georges Simenon
shelf.creator: Georges Simenon
shelf.why: Amit says Simenon’s work keeps re­turn­ing to the idea that no per­son can fully com­mu­ni­cate him­self to an­other, which he sees as one of humanity’s great prob­lems.

shelf.title: The Nighttime Lights of Russia — Ep 116 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How satel­lite night-lights let Indian re­searchers see into the Russian econ­omy in ways tra­di­tional sta­tis­tics never could, part of the show’s se­ries on mea­sure­ment.

shelf.title: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us — Ep 117 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Part of the show’s se­ries on mea­sure­ment: how new data, such as borrowers’ phone top-up habits, is re­plac­ing the bank manager’s per­sonal judge­ment.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

laughs.text: After not­ing that more men search for porn than for weather, Amit tells Ajay he must search a lot for weather: ‘But you can’t jerk off to clouds. So there’s an un­der­stand­able rea­son for that.’

On the Australian au­to­com­plete re­sults ‘an open marriage’ and ‘an open mar­riage novel’: ‘from this I can only gather that Australians want to read books about the things that they are both­ered about.’

On the name ‘WHMSI’: ‘I was call­ing it the Whimsy Index till I re­al­ized that the I at the end of it stands for index. So it would be like call­ing it When Harry Met Sally Index Index, which we don’t want to do.’

Gabriel García Márquez’s three selves (pub­lic, pri­vate, se­cret). Amit adds that the pri­vate self is known to a hand­ful of in­ti­mates, ‘Dunbar’s smaller num­ber, not one fifty, but five’, and the se­cret self is known to no­body ‘ex­cept Google Baba’.

Stephens-Davidowitz’s line: ‘Facebook is dig­i­tal brag-to-my-friends-about-how-good-my-life-is serum,’ where ev­ery­one seems hap­pily mar­ried and on hol­i­day in the Caribbean, while in re­al­ity peo­ple are ig­nor­ing calls from spouses they haven’t slept with in years.
